[Thesis]{.type-badge}

In 1987, Robert Solow wrote the most-quoted sentence in
productivity economics: you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity
statistics [@solow1987]. Thirty-eight years later, an MIT team reported that **95% of
enterprise AI pilots** show no measurable return [@mit2025]. Both times the consensus
reached for the same verdict — overhyped. Both times, it was staring at the *trough of a
J-curve* and calling it a cliff.

::: {.tape}
**95%** — enterprise generative-AI pilots with no measurable P&L impact<br>
`MIT Project NANDA · 2025`
:::

Paul David caught this rhyme a century back [@david1990].
Electricity arrived in the 1880s. Factories electrified fast — and then productivity
*didn't move for forty years*. The reason wasn't the dynamo. It was that firms first bolted
electric motors onto the old steam-era layout: one big motor still turning a maze of line
shafts and belts. The gains only came once they tore the shafts out and rebuilt around the
*unit drive* — a motor on every machine, the floor plan freed, the single-story plant.
Reorganization, not electrification, was the productivity event. And reorganization takes a
generation.

Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson turned that history into a
model [@brs2018]. A general-purpose technology demands enormous *intangible* investment —
new processes, business models, retrained people — that the national accounts simply don't
count. So while a firm builds that hidden capital, its measured output is too low and its
productivity looks worse than reality. Later, when the intangibles pay off, output rises
against costs that were expensed years ago, and productivity looks *better* than reality.
Plot the gap and you get a J:

::: {.pull-source}
"…this leads to an underestimation of productivity growth in the early years of a new GPT,
and… later, when the benefits of intangible investments are harvested, productivity growth
will be overestimated."

[— Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson, 2018]{.attribution}
:::

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

_jc = pd.read_parquet(Path("../../analysis/outputs/jcurve_sample.parquet"))
_jc["date"] = pd.to_datetime(_jc["date"]).dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
ojs_define(jc_data=_jc.to_dict(orient="records"))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
import { Plot } from "npm:@observablehq/plot"
jc = jc_data.map(d => ({...d, date: new Date(d.date)}))
jcLast = jc[jc.length - 1]
jcIdx = key => jc.map(d => ({date: d.date, value: d[key] / jc[0][key] * 100}))
jcRaw = key => jc.map(d => ({date: d.date, value: d[key]}))
jcPct = v => `${v > 0 ? "+" : ""}${v.toFixed(0)}%`

jcTwoLine = (a, b, w, h, extra = {}) => Plot.plot({
  width: w, height: h, marginLeft: 30, marginBottom: 20, marginTop: 12, marginRight: 10,
  x: {type: "utc", label: null, ticks: 4, tickFormat: "%y"},
  y: {label: null, grid: true, ...(extra.y || {})},
  style: {fontFamily: "DM Mono, monospace", fontSize: "9px"},
  marks: [
    ...(extra.baseline != null ? [Plot.ruleY([extra.baseline], {stroke: "#C8C3B8", strokeDasharray: "2,3"})] : []),
    Plot.lineY(a.data, {x: "date", y: "value", stroke: a.color, strokeWidth: 1.9}),
    Plot.lineY(b.data, {x: "date", y: "value", stroke: b.color, strokeWidth: 1.9}),
    Plot.dot([a.data[a.data.length - 1]], {x: "date", y: "value", r: 3, fill: a.color}),
    Plot.dot([b.data[b.data.length - 1]], {x: "date", y: "value", r: 3, fill: b.color})
  ]
})

jcInputs = jcTwoLine({data: jcIdx("adoption"), color: "#7C6FB5"}, {data: jcIdx("it_investment"), color: "#4A6FA5"}, 360, 190)
jcPayoff = jcTwoLine({data: jcRaw("productivity"), color: "#3A7D5E"}, {data: jcRaw("tfp"), color: "#9A8F7A"}, 360, 190, {baseline: 100, y: {domain: [92, 122]}})

jcRecalcData = jc.map(d => ({date: d.date, meas: d.productivity, adj: d.productivity_adj}))
jcRecalc = Plot.plot({
  width: 680, height: 240, marginLeft: 32, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 14, marginRight: 64,
  x: {type: "utc", label: null, ticks: 5, tickFormat: "%Y"},
  y: {label: null, grid: true},
  style: {fontFamily: "DM Mono, monospace", fontSize: "10px"},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(jcRecalcData, {x: "date", y1: "meas", y2: "adj", fill: "#3A7D5E", fillOpacity: 0.10}),
    Plot.lineY(jcRecalcData, {x: "date", y: "meas", stroke: "#6A6A6A", strokeWidth: 1.8}),
    Plot.lineY(jcRecalcData, {x: "date", y: "adj", stroke: "#3A7D5E", strokeWidth: 1.8, strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.text([jcRecalcData[jcRecalcData.length - 1]], {x: "date", y: "adj", text: ["adjusted"], dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 9, fill: "#3A7D5E"}),
    Plot.text([jcRecalcData[jcRecalcData.length - 1]], {x: "date", y: "meas", text: ["measured"], dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 9, fill: "#6A6A6A"})
  ]
})
```

Which brings us to the present, and to a productivity theorist from an unlikely address:
Citadel Securities. Its *Tokenomics* note [@citadel2026] describes AI as rationed by
physical inputs — compute, power, cooling — bifurcating into a frontier only deep balance
sheets can afford and a cheap "good-enough" tier for everyone else. Strip the AI vocabulary
and it is textbook GPT diffusion: the concentrated, capital-hungry early phase, exactly
where David's dynamo sat in 1900. The 95% of pilots that "fail" are firms that bought the
model and bolted it onto the old workflow. **Group drive, not unit drive.**

None of this proves AI will pay off. It says the current disappointment is *uninformative* —
which is precisely what the bottom of a J-curve looks like from inside.

*What would prove me wrong:* if total factor productivity in the most AI-exposed industries
shows no J — no dip, no recovery — five years out, the reorganization-lag story is dead, and
the skeptics were right that this one is different. It's a measurable bet, and the data
(BLS total factor productivity by industry) will settle it. I intend to keep score.

## The scoreboard

The bet, made watchable. Inputs on one side, payoff on the other. If it's a J-curve,
the first pair races ahead while the second stays pinned to the floor — until the
reorganization finally pays.
